```{r setup}
slope <- function(x, y) sum((x - mean(x)) * (y - mean(y))) / sum((x - mean(x))^2)
dm    <- function(z, g) z - ave(z, g)
nickell <- function(a, m) {                            # Nickell (1981) plim of FE bias, m = T-1 AR obs
  if (m < 3) return(-(1 + a) / 2)
  A <- 1 - (1 / m) * (1 - a^m) / (1 - a)
  B <- 1 - (2 * a / ((1 - a) * (m - 1))) * (1 - (1 - a^m) / (m * (1 - a)))
  -((1 + a) / (m - 1)) * A / B
}
gen_panel <- function(N, T, rho, su = 1, se = 1, on_target = TRUE) {   # T x N matrix of levels
  u <- rnorm(N, 0, su)                                 # on_target: start at own long-run level
  y <- (if (on_target) u / (1 - rho) else 0) + rnorm(N, 0, se / sqrt(1 - rho^2))
  M <- matrix(0, T, N); M[1, ] <- y
  for (t in 2:T) M[t, ] <- rho * M[t - 1, ] + u + rnorm(N, 0, se)
  M
}
ols_fe <- function(M) {
  T <- nrow(M); N <- ncol(M); id <- rep(1:N, each = T - 1)
  yc <- as.vector(M[2:T, , drop = FALSE]); yl <- as.vector(M[1:(T - 1), , drop = FALSE])
  c(ols = slope(yl, yc), fe = slope(dm(yl, id), dm(yc, id)))
}
estimators <- function(M) {                            # OLS, FE, Anderson-Hsiao, one-step difference and system GMM
  T <- nrow(M); N <- ncol(M)
  b <- ols_fe(M)
  dY  <- M[3:T, , drop = FALSE] - M[2:(T - 1), , drop = FALSE]
  dY1 <- M[2:(T - 1), , drop = FALSE] - M[1:(T - 2), , drop = FALSE]
  Z2  <- M[1:(T - 2), , drop = FALSE]
  ah  <- sum(Z2 * dY) / sum(Z2 * dY1)
  m <- T - 2; L <- m * (m + 1) / 2
  H <- diag(2, m); H[abs(row(H) - col(H)) == 1] <- -1
  Hs <- rbind(cbind(H, matrix(0, m, m)), cbind(matrix(0, m, m), diag(m)))
  ZHZ <- matrix(0, L, L); ZX <- numeric(L); ZY <- numeric(L)
  SZ <- matrix(0, L + m, L + m); SX <- numeric(L + m); SY <- numeric(L + m)
  for (i in 1:N) {
    Zi <- matrix(0, m, L); c0 <- 0
    for (s in 1:m) { Zi[s, c0 + 1:s] <- M[1:s, i]; c0 <- c0 + s }
    ZHZ <- ZHZ + crossprod(Zi, H %*% Zi)
    ZX  <- ZX + crossprod(Zi, dY1[, i]); ZY <- ZY + crossprod(Zi, dY[, i])
    Zs <- rbind(cbind(Zi, matrix(0, m, m)), cbind(matrix(0, m, L), diag(dY1[, i], m)))
    Xs <- c(dY1[, i], M[2:(T - 1), i]); Ys <- c(dY[, i], M[3:T, i])
    SZ <- SZ + crossprod(Zs, Hs %*% Zs); SX <- SX + crossprod(Zs, Xs); SY <- SY + crossprod(Zs, Ys)
  }
  W  <- solve(ZHZ); ab  <- as.numeric((t(ZX) %*% W  %*% ZY) / (t(ZX) %*% W  %*% ZX))
  Ws <- solve(SZ);  sys <- as.numeric((t(SX) %*% Ws %*% SY) / (t(SX) %*% Ws %*% SX))
  c(b, ah = ah, ab = ab, sys = sys)
}
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
```

## Where we left off

- Fixed effects removes everything permanent about a firm. The price was **strict exogeneity**: today's shock must not feed into tomorrow's regressors.
- Leverage, payout, cash, investment all depend on **their own past**. Put last year's $Y$ on the right-hand side and strict exogeneity is not doubtful.


## The plan

1. **The problem.** OLS and fixed effects both get persistence wrong --- and we know which way.
2. **The fix.** A longer lag of the same variable, used as an instrument.
3. **When the fix fails.** Persistent series, large firm effects --- exactly the finance case --- and the repair.
4. **In practice.** Leverage adjustment, the code, what to report.

# 1. The Problem

## Most things in finance drift

They do not jump to a target. They close part of the gap each year.
$$
Y_{it} \;=\; \rho\,Y_{i,t-1} + \delta D_{it} + u_i + \varepsilon_{it}, \qquad |\rho| < 1
$$


## Fixed effects manufactures mean reversion

Demeaning subtracts each firm's *average* error from every year's error. A lucky shock last year raised $Y_{i,t-1}$ --- and sits inside that average.
$$
\underbrace{Y_{i,t-1} - \bar Y_{i}}_{\text{regressor: contains } +\varepsilon_{i,t-1}}
\qquad
\underbrace{\varepsilon_{it} - \bar\varepsilon_{i}}_{\text{error: contains } -\varepsilon_{i,t-1}/T}
$$

- The year the regressor is high is a year the error has been pushed down. The fitted slope tilts **down**: **Nickell (1981) bias**, of order $1/T$.
- Same $\rho = 0$ experiment, $T = 5$: $\hat\rho_{\text{FE}} = `r sprintf("%.2f", z0["fe"])`$, which is $-1/(T-1)$. OLS invented persistence; demeaning invents reversion.
- It happens **even without any firm effect**: demeaning alone does it.

## Both biases in one picture

```{r bias-T}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| out-width: 82%
#| fig-align: center
set.seed(20260202)
rho <- 0.6; N <- 4000; Ts <- c(3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 15, 20, 30)
r <- sapply(Ts, function(T) ols_fe(gen_panel(N, T, rho)))
brk <- r[, Ts == 5]
par(mar = c(2.6, 3.2, 0.3, 0.3), mgp = c(1.7, 0.5, 0), cex = 0.9)
plot(NA, xlim = c(3, 30), ylim = c(-0.3, 1), xlab = "years per firm, T", ylab = expression(hat(rho)), las = 1, log = "x", xaxt = "n")
axis(1, at = c(3, 5, 10, 20, 30))
abline(h = rho, lty = 2); abline(h = 0, col = "grey80")
lines(Ts, r["ols", ], type = "b", pch = 16, lwd = 2)
lines(Ts, r["fe", ], type = "b", pch = 17, lwd = 2)
lines(3:30, rho + sapply(2:29, function(m) nickell(rho, m)), col = "grey50", lty = 3)
text(30, r["ols", 9] + 0.08, "pooled OLS", adj = 1, cex = 0.9)
text(30, r["fe", 9] - 0.09, "fixed effects", adj = 1, cex = 0.9)
text(3.05, rho + 0.07, expression("truth " * rho == 0.6), adj = 0, cex = 0.9)
```

$\rho = 0.6$, $4{,}000$ firms, $\sigma_u = \sigma_\varepsilon$. Dotted: Nickell's formula for the fixed-effects plim.

- **OLS never moves.** Heterogeneity is not resolved by more years.
- **Fixed effects heals, slowly.** At $T = 3$ it is *negative* for a process with persistence $0.6$; at $T = 30$ it is still short. Finance panels are $10$--$20$ years. The more persistent the series, the slower the bias leaves.

## Two wrongs that fence in the truth

$$
\hat\rho_{\text{FE}} \;<\; \rho \;<\; \hat\rho_{\text{OLS}}
$$

- Neither is consistent, but you know the **sign** of each bias. At $T = 5$ above: $`r f2(brk["fe"])` < 0.60 < `r f2(brk["ols"])`$. Wide --- and honest.
- **The standard first move** (Bond 2002): run both *before* anything clever, and keep both numbers. They are the goalposts.
- **Any estimator you trust must land between them.** One that lands outside is telling you an assumption failed --- before you interpret a single coefficient.

# 2. The Fix

## Differencing kills the firm effect --- and shows the real problem

$$
\Delta Y_{it} \;=\; \rho\,\Delta Y_{i,t-1} + \delta\,\Delta D_{it} + \Delta\varepsilon_{it}
$$

```{r timeline}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 1.75
#| out-width: 80%
#| fig-align: center
par(mar = c(0.2, 8.5, 1.6, 0.5), cex = 0.95)
plot(NA, xlim = c(-3.5, 0.5), ylim = c(0.5, 3.5), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
rect(-1.45, 0.55, -0.55, 3.45, col = "grey90", border = NA)
axis(3, at = -3:0, labels = c(expression(epsilon[t-3]), expression(epsilon[t-2]), expression(epsilon[t-1]), expression(epsilon[t])), tick = FALSE, line = -0.8)
axis(2, at = 3:1, tick = FALSE, las = 1, line = -0.5,
     labels = c(expression("regressor " * Delta * Y[i*","*t-1]), expression("error " * Delta * epsilon[it]), expression("instrument " * Y[i*","*t-2])))
points(c(-3, -2), c(3, 3), pch = 1, cex = 1.3); points(-1, 3, pch = 16, cex = 1.6)
points(c(-1, 0), c(2, 2), pch = 16, cex = 1.6)
points(c(-3, -2), c(1, 1), pch = 1, cex = 1.3)
text(-1, 0.75, "shared", cex = 0.85)
```

\vspace{-0.3em}

- $u_i$ is gone. But the regressor $\Delta Y_{i,t-1}$ contains last year's shock, and so does the error $\Delta\varepsilon_{it}$ --- **with a minus sign**. Differencing is not the fix; it is where the fixed-effects bias comes from.
- **Go back one more year.** $Y_{i,t-2}$ is built from shocks dated $t-2$ and earlier: it shares nothing with the error, yet it is part of $\Delta Y_{i,t-1}$, so it predicts the regressor.
- That is **Anderson--Hsiao (1982)**: IV on the differenced equation, $Y_{i,t-2}$ as instrument. **A broken regressor and a valid instrument are one date apart.**

## Arellano--Bond: use every lag you have

At date $t$, *every* $Y$ dated $t-2$ or earlier is a valid instrument. Use them all (Holtz-Eakin, Newey and Rosen 1988; Arellano and Bond 1991):

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Differenced equation at & valid instruments for $\Delta Y_{i,t-1}$ & count \\
\midrule
$t = 3$ & $Y_{i1}$ & 1 \\
$t = 4$ & $Y_{i1},\, Y_{i2}$ & 2 \\
$t = T$ & $Y_{i1},\, \dots,\, Y_{i,T-2}$ & $T-2$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- $(T-1)(T-2)/2$ instruments in all, so the estimator is **GMM**. Gain: Anderson--Hsiao with one instrument is very noisy; this is far tighter.
- Cost: the count grows with $T^2$ --- $91$ at $T = 15$, $406$ at $T = 30$. **Too many instruments** (Roodman 2009) overfit the regressor, contamination included, and GMM slides back toward OLS on the differenced equation, which is biased *down*. Hansen's $J$ loses the power to object.
- Remedies: **cap** the lag depth, **collapse** the instrument set to one column per lag. Keep the count well below $N$, and report it.

## What to report, and why

- **Windmeijer (2005) standard errors.** Two-step GMM is efficient but its standard errors are far too small in finite samples. One-step robust and two-step Windmeijer should agree; if they do not, something is weak.
- **AR(2) test on $\Delta\varepsilon$.** AR(1) is expected --- adjacent differences share $\varepsilon_{i,t-1}$. AR(2) must be *absent*: it appears only if $\varepsilon$ itself is serially correlated, and then $Y_{i,t-2}$ shares a shock with the error and **every instrument fails**. This is the test of the identifying assumption.
- **Hansen $J$**, with the instrument count next to it. $J$ is informative only when the count is small relative to $N$.
- **The bracket.** Below $\hat\rho_{\text{FE}}$: weak or too many instruments. Above $\hat\rho_{\text{OLS}}$: a violated assumption --- next section shows one.

# 3. When the Fix Fails

## Weak instruments: a level barely predicts a change

```{r gamma-plot}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 1.9
#| out-width: 70%
#| fig-align: center
gam <- function(rho, r) { k <- (1 - rho) / (1 + rho); (rho - 1) * k / (k + r) }
rg <- seq(0, 0.99, by = 0.01)
par(mar = c(2.6, 3.2, 0.3, 0.3), mgp = c(1.7, 0.5, 0), cex = 0.9)
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(-1, 0), xlab = expression(rho), ylab = "first-stage coefficient", las = 1)
abline(h = 0, col = "grey60")
for (k in 1:3) { vr <- c(0.25, 1, 4)[k]; lines(rg, gam(rg, vr), lwd = 2, lty = k) }
legend("bottomright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, lty = 1:3, cex = 0.9,
       legend = c(expression(sigma[u]^2/sigma[epsilon]^2 == 0.25), expression(sigma[u]^2/sigma[epsilon]^2 == 1), expression(sigma[u]^2/sigma[epsilon]^2 == 4)))
```

Each year a firm closes a fraction $1-\rho$ of its gap to its own long-run level:
$$
\Delta Y_{i,t-1} \;=\; -(1-\rho)\,\underbrace{\big(Y_{i,t-2} - \tfrac{u_i}{1-\rho}\big)}_{\text{gap}} + \varepsilon_{i,t-1}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\gamma \;=\; (\rho-1)\,\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\text{gap})}{\operatorname{Var}(Y_{i,t-2})}
$$

- The level predicts the change **only through the gap**; its height predicts nothing. **Two ways to die:** $\rho \to 1$, the gap closes too slowly to matter; large $\sigma^2_u$, the level is mostly height (Blundell and Bond 1998).
- $\gamma = `r f2(gam(0.6, 1))`$ at $\rho = 0.6$; $`r sprintf("%.3f", gam(0.95, 1))`$ at $\rho = 0.95$. Leverage, payout and cash live in the right-hand third. **The instrument is weakest exactly where you need it.**

## System GMM: instrument the level with the change

Blundell and Bond (1998): keep the differenced equation, and **add the levels equation**, instrumented the other way round:
$$
Y_{it} = \rho\,Y_{i,t-1} + u_i + \varepsilon_{it}, \qquad \text{instrument } Y_{i,t-1} \text{ with } \Delta Y_{i,t-1}
$$

- **Why it helps.** A level cannot predict a random walk's next step --- but **a firm that just rose is high**. The first-stage coefficient of $Y_{i,t-1}$ on $\Delta Y_{i,t-1}$ is $\tfrac12$ for *every* $\rho$. It never dies.
- **What it costs.** The levels error contains $u_i$, so a firm's changes must say nothing about its permanent level: $\mathbb{E}[\Delta Y_{i,t-1}\,u_i] = 0$. True in the two-firm picture *because both firms started at their own long-run levels* --- **mean stationarity**.
- **When to doubt it.** Firms observed from IPO start away from target and converge; a panel that starts after a crisis has everyone off target together. Then rising *does* reveal a high-$u_i$ firm, and the extra instruments are invalid.

## Every estimator, on one line

```{r one-line}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.4
#| out-width: 100%
#| fig-align: center
set.seed(1)
sims <- list(a = replicate(200, estimators(gen_panel(500, 6, 0.6))),
             b = replicate(200, estimators(gen_panel(500, 6, 0.95))),
             c = replicate(200, estimators(gen_panel(500, 6, 0.95, on_target = FALSE))))
med  <- lapply(sims, function(s) apply(s, 1, median))
labs <- c("OLS", "FE", "AH", "AB", "System")
ttl  <- c(expression(rho == 0.6), expression(rho == 0.95), expression(rho == 0.95 * ", firms start off target"))
tru  <- c(0.6, 0.95, 0.95); xl <- c(0, 1.3)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(2.4, 3.6, 1.4, 0.4), mgp = c(1.4, 0.4, 0), cex = 1)
for (k in 1:3) {
  s <- sims[[k]]; q <- apply(s, 1, quantile, c(.1, .5, .9)); y <- 5:1
  plot(NA, xlim = xl, ylim = c(0.5, 5.5), yaxt = "n", xlab = expression(hat(rho)), ylab = "", main = ttl[k], cex.main = 1)
  axis(2, at = y, labels = labs, las = 1, tick = FALSE)
  rect(q[2, "fe"], 0, q[2, "ols"], 6, col = "grey90", border = NA)
  abline(v = tru[k], lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  lo <- pmax(q[1, ], xl[1]); hi <- pmin(q[3, ], xl[2])
  segments(lo, y, hi, y, lwd = 2)
  out_l <- q[1, ] < xl[1]; out_h <- q[3, ] > xl[2]
  if (any(out_l)) arrows(xl[1] + 0.08, y[out_l], xl[1], y[out_l], length = 0.05, lwd = 2)
  if (any(out_h)) arrows(xl[2] - 0.08, y[out_h], xl[2], y[out_h], length = 0.05, lwd = 2)
  points(q[2, ], y, pch = 19, cex = 1.1)
  box()
}
```

\scriptsize $500$ firms, $T = 6$, $200$ draws. Dots: medians; bars: 10th--90th percentiles; shaded: the bracket; dashed: the truth. \normalsize

- **$\rho = 0.6$:** every IV lands in the bracket, near the truth. **$\rho = 0.95$:** the difference estimators collapse; system GMM holds ($`r f2(med$b["sys"])`$).
- **Firms start off target:** Arellano--Bond recovers ($`r f2(med$c["ab"])`$); system GMM lands at $`r f2(med$c["sys"])`$, *above OLS* --- and the bracket catches it. **Each estimator fails exactly when its own assumption does.**

## Long panels: a different route

- **Bias-corrected fixed effects.** Nickell's bias has a known formula, so subtract it: estimate FE, correct at $\hat\rho$, iterate (Kiviet 1995; Bruno 2005; Stata `xtlsdvc`). No instruments, so nothing to be weak --- but the other regressors must be strictly exogenous, which finance controls rarely are.
- **Horse race on finance-like panels** --- short, persistent, unbalanced (Flannery and Hankins 2013): bias-corrected FE and system GMM generally reliable; difference GMM frequently not.

\vspace{0.3em}

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\toprule
If & then \\
\midrule
$T \le 10$, $\rho$ moderate & Arellano--Bond, with the diagnostics \\
$\rho$ near one & system GMM, with mean stationarity defended \\
$T \ge 20$, exogenous controls & bias-corrected fixed effects \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

# 4. In Practice

## Case study: how fast do firms adjust leverage?

The partial-adjustment model is our equation with $Y$ = leverage and $1-\rho$ the **speed of adjustment**.

\begin{center}\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
Paper & Estimator & $\hat\rho$ & speed $1-\hat\rho$ \\
\midrule
Fama and French (2002) & pooled (Fama--MacBeth) & $\approx 0.85$ & $\approx 7$--$18\%$ \\
Flannery and Rangan (2006) & FE, lagged leverage instrumented & $\approx 0.66$ & $\approx 34\%$ \\
Lemmon, Roberts and Zender (2008) & system GMM & $\approx 0.75$ & $\approx 25\%$ \\
Huang and Ritter (2009) & long differencing & $\approx 0.80$ & $\approx 17$--$23\%$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- **The ordering is the bracket.** Fixed effects reports the *fastest* adjustment, pooled estimation the *slowest*; the IV-type estimates sit between.
- Whether firms rebalance toward targets or just drift **turned on the bias this lecture is about**: a half-life of $1.7$ years and one of $5$ are different theories of the firm.
- Caveat: samples, periods and leverage definitions differ across the papers. The ordering is suggestive, not a controlled horse race.

## The code

```stata
* 1. The bracket first -- and keep both numbers
reg   y L.y x i.year, cluster(firm)
xtreg y L.y x i.year, fe cluster(firm)

* 2. Difference GMM (Arellano-Bond): two-step, Windmeijer SEs, lags 2-4 of y
xtabond y x i.year, lags(1) maxldep(3) twostep vce(robust)
estat abond                       // AR(1) expected; AR(2) must be absent

* 3. Same, with collapsed instruments and the Hansen test (Roodman's xtabond2)
xtabond2 y L.y x i.year, gmm(y, lag(2 4) collapse) iv(x i.year) ///
         noleveleq twostep robust
*    x predetermined rather than exogenous? iv(x ...) -> gmm(x, lag(1 3) collapse)

* 4. System GMM -- only after you have defended mean stationarity
xtdpdsys y x i.year, lags(1) maxldep(3) twostep vce(robust)

* 5. Long T, exogenous x: bias-corrected fixed effects
xtlsdvc y x, initial(ab) bias(3) vcov(50)
```

- R: `plm::pgmm()` with `transformation = "d"` or `"ld"`. Simulation to grade them against a known $\rho$: `06b_dynamic_panel_sim.do` (one draw in the backup).

## Conclusion

1. **A lagged $Y$ is endogenous by construction.** The question is whether a firm is high because it *was* high, or because it *is* high.
2. **OLS says "was high" too often; fixed effects too rarely.** Run both first: **the bracket is the goalposts.**
3. **The fix is a longer lag of the same variable.** $Y_{i,t-2}$ is one date too early to be contaminated. Arellano--Bond uses all such lags; cap and collapse them.
4. **The fix fails when the series is persistent or firm effects are large** --- the normal case in finance. Then system GMM, if firms sit at their own long-run levels; or bias-corrected FE, if $T$ allows.
5. **Each estimator fails exactly when its own assumption does**, and the bracket usually shows it. Ask of every estimate: *which way is it wrong?*

- Windmeijer, F. (2005). A Finite Sample Correction for the Variance of Linear Efficient Two-Step GMM Estimators. *Journal of Econometrics* 126(1), 25--51.

# Backup

## B1. The date rule, and the Nickell bias at $T = 3$

$Y_{is}$ is built from $u_i$ and shocks dated $s$ and earlier. If $\varepsilon$ is serially uncorrelated and unrelated to $u_i$:
$$
\mathbb{E}[Y_{is}\,\varepsilon_{it}] = 0 \;\;\text{for } t > s, \qquad \mathbb{E}[Y_{is}\,\varepsilon_{is}] = \sigma^2_\varepsilon
$$

With $T = 3$ there is one differenced observation per firm, so $\hat\rho_{\text{FE}}$ is least squares on $\Delta Y_{i3} = \rho\,\Delta Y_{i2} + \Delta\varepsilon_{i3}$:
$$
\operatorname{plim}(\hat\rho_{\text{FE}} - \rho) = \frac{\mathbb{E}[\Delta Y_{i2}\,\Delta\varepsilon_{i3}]}{\mathbb{E}[(\Delta Y_{i2})^2]}
= \frac{-\sigma^2_\varepsilon}{2\sigma^2_\varepsilon/(1+\rho)} = -\,\frac{1+\rho}{2}
$$

- Numerator: expand $(Y_{i2} - Y_{i1})(\varepsilon_{i3} - \varepsilon_{i2})$. Three products pair a $Y$ with a *later* shock: zero. One pairs $Y_{i2}$ with its own shock, with a minus sign: $-\sigma^2_\varepsilon$.
- Denominator: $u_i$ cancels in a difference; what is left has variance $2\sigma^2_\varepsilon/(1+\rho)$.
- The plim is negative for every $\rho < 1$. (Hansen 2022, §17.37.)

## B2. One date apart, as a table

Each cell is $\mathbb{E}[\text{row} \times \text{column}]$; the last column is the first minus the second.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
 & $\varepsilon_{it}$ & $\varepsilon_{i,t-1}$ & $\Delta\varepsilon_{it}$ \\
\midrule
$Y_{i,t-1}$ & $0$ (later shock) & $\boldsymbol{\sigma^2_\varepsilon}$ (same date) & $-\sigma^2_\varepsilon$ \\
$Y_{i,t-2}$ & $0$ (later shock) & $0$ (later shock) & $0$ \\
\midrule
$\Delta Y_{i,t-1} = Y_{i,t-1} - Y_{i,t-2}$ & & & $\boldsymbol{-\sigma^2_\varepsilon}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- **Validity.** The regressor inherits the one same-date term; the instrument, one year older, has none.
- **Relevance.** $\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{i,t-2}, \Delta Y_{i,t-1}) = -\sigma^2_\varepsilon/(1+\rho) \ne 0$ --- but small when $\rho$ is near one, which is the weak-instrument problem of Section 3.
- **The zero row needs serially uncorrelated $\varepsilon$.** If the truth is AR(2) and you fit AR(1), $\varepsilon_{i,t-2}$ inside $Y_{i,t-2}$ predicts $\varepsilon_{i,t-1}$ and the instrument is invalid. That is what the AR(2) test checks.

## B3. Try it: simulate, estimate, grade

```{r stata-draw}
# One draw of 06b_dynamic_panel_sim.do (Stata 19, seed 20260202, N = 500, T = 8)
sd_draw <- rbind(ols = c("0.918", "0.999", "1.083"),
                 fe  = c("0.334", "0.592", "0.840"),
                 ah  = c("0.596", "1.077", "1.004"),
                 ab  = c("0.609", "0.824", "0.966"),
                 sys = c("0.589", "1.010", "\\textbf{1.150}"))
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="66%"}

```stata
clear all
set seed 20260202
local rho = 0.6                      // then 0.95
set obs 500
gen firm = _n
gen u = rnormal()                    // firm effect
* start each firm at its own long-run level
gen y = u/(1-`rho') + rnormal(0, 1/sqrt(1-`rho'^2))
expand 8
bysort firm: gen year = _n
xtset firm year
by firm: replace y = `rho'*y[_n-1] + u + rnormal() if _n > 1

reg   y L.y, vce(cluster firm)                    // up
xtreg y L.y, fe vce(cluster firm)                 // down
ivregress 2sls D.y (LD.y = L2.y), vce(cluster firm)
xtabond  y, lags(1) maxldep(3) twostep vce(robust)
xtdpdsys y, lags(1) maxldep(3) twostep vce(robust)
```

## B4. A reporting checklist

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{R{5.2cm}R{7.4cm}}
\toprule
Report & Because \\
\midrule
$\hat\rho_{\text{OLS}}$ and $\hat\rho_{\text{FE}}$ & the bracket; your estimate must sit inside it \\
AR(1) and AR(2) tests & AR(2) tests the identifying assumption \\
Hansen $J$, the instrument count, lag depth, collapsed or not & $J$ is informative only when the count is small relative to $N$ \\
one-step and two-step (Windmeijer) side by side & disagreement signals weakness \\
difference vs.\ system GMM, with mean stationarity defended & they rest on different assumptions \\
what $D$ is assumed to be (exogenous / predetermined / endogenous) & it determines which lags of $D$ are valid instruments \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

## B5. Bracketing $\delta$: lagged $Y$ or fixed effects?

When you are unsure **which model** is right --- lagged $Y$, or fixed effects --- and what you care about is $\delta$, the two estimates bracket it too.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
If the truth is & and you estimate & then $\hat\delta$ is \\
\midrule
the lagged model & fixed effects      & too \textbf{high} \\
the fixed effects model & the lagged model & too \textbf{low} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- Intuition: under the lagged model, a treated firm's $Y_{i,t-1}$ already carries part of the effect, and fixed effects, ignoring it, attributes that part to $D$. Under the fixed-effects model, the lagged $Y$ absorbs part of the firm effect *and* part of the treatment.
- Angrist and Pischke (2009, §5.4): report both. If they agree on the sign and roughly on the size, the question of which model is right matters less than you feared.
